title: The line
hook: the line in the dust; the beggar at the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry: a dying demon in Rama's voice, and Lakshmana driven from the hut. Your line was check the voice. Now Sita is alone. Almost. Day fifty-one.

Before Lakshmana leaves, in the version many people in India grew up with, he does one last thing. He takes an arrow and draws a line in the dust, all the way around the hut. Stay inside this line, he tells Sita. Whatever happens. Whoever comes. Nothing evil can cross it. Then he runs into the forest. The clearing goes quiet. And a few minutes later, a holy man comes walking out of the trees. An old wandering ascetic, with a staff and a begging bowl, chanting softly. He stops at the edge of the line. And he asks, very politely, for food.
screen: `A LINE IN THE DUST.` → `STAY INSIDE IT.` → `A HOLY MAN AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The holy man is Ravana in disguise. And in the telling many people know, he can't cross the line. So he needs Sita to cross it. He asks for alms. She offers them from inside. He says: a holy man can't take food from someone behind a barrier. Come out and give it properly, or I'll leave, and you'll have turned away a guest. Now, in this tradition, hospitality is sacred. There's an old teaching: treat the guest as God. Sita has been raised on it. Turning away a holy man at your door is almost unthinkable. So she lifts her foot, and steps over the line. That line has a name: Lakshmana rekha. Rekha means line. Lakshmana's line. And here's the honest part. It isn't in Valmiki's Ramayana. In Valmiki, Lakshmana just leaves, and Sita welcomes the disguised Ravana as a guest, with water and food. The line appears in later retellings, and it's become so loved that many people are surprised it isn't in the oldest text. The tradition kept growing, and it grew this. Today, Lakshmana rekha is an everyday phrase across India. People use it for a boundary you must not cross: in a family, in politics, in a friendship. Here's what the story knows. A good line doesn't hold by being strong. It holds because you stay behind it, even when crossing looks kind, and polite, and right. The trouble wasn't that Sita was careless. It was that the one voice trying to get her across used her best quality against her. Hold the line.
screen: `RAVANA NEEDS HER TO CROSS.` · `TREAT THE GUEST AS GOD.` · `NOT IN VALMIKI. LATER, AND LOVED.` · `A LINE YOU MUST NOT CROSS.` · then, large: `HOLD THE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: your own line, and who crossed it. Sit and breathe. What's one line you've drawn for yourself? About your time, your body, your values, what you'll put up with. Picture it drawn in the dust around you. Now remember a time someone talked you across it, maybe politely, maybe by appealing to your kindness. No blame. Just see it clearly. Then redraw the line, slowly, in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana rekha. Lakshmana's line: drawn around the hut in later tellings, and now an everyday phrase for a limit you must not cross.
Your line: hold the line. Today, when someone asks you to cross one of yours, even kindly, stay where you are. Day fifty-one.

howItsDone: In everyday speech across India, a Lakshmana rekha is a boundary that must not be crossed; in many Ramlila performances the line around the hut is a well-known moment, even though it does not appear in Valmiki's text.

fork.setup: you're Sita, alone inside the line. a holy man says he can't take food across a barrier, and will leave if you don't come out. what do you do?
options: step over the line to give him food properly.
fork.reveal: in the telling many people know, she steps over to honor a guest. the holy man is Ravana.

original.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: Lakshmana's line (rekha), a boundary not to be crossed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic line around a hut.
what it means: a boundary that holds only if you stay behind it, even when crossing looks kind.
what a scholar hears: the rekha is absent from Valmiki and appears in later retellings; its fame shows how the Ramayana tradition keeps growing.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 45–46 (Lakshmana leaves; Ravana comes as an ascetic and is welcomed as a guest)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (treat the guest as a god)

notes: The Lakshmana rekha is absent from Valmiki. Its earliest attestation is uncertain; it is often linked to later regional retellings, and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas has Mandodari allude to Lakshmana's line in the Lanka Kanda. Keeper/scholar to confirm and, if desired, name the source.
'Treat the guest as God' (atithi devo bhava) is from Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2; paraphrased. Confirm.
Ravana's argument (can't take alms across a barrier) follows popular tellings; confirm.

Reviewer softened 'most people' to 'many people' (three places) and the Ramlila line in howItsDone ('one of the most anticipated moments' to 'a well-known moment'); how widely the rekha episode is staged and known is not settled. Confirm.
